Impact of Chinese Silk on India Silk Industry 
*136. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: 
SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: 
Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether silk items from China are flooding the Indian market, 
thereby jeopardizing the interests of indigenously produced silk; and 
(b) if so, the details and how this onslaught is proposed to be countered 
to protect the Indian silk industry? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir, there has been increase in imports of raw silk, silk 
yarn and Fabrics from China in the last three years. Import of raw silk from 
China has grown from 6317 in 2001-02 to 7296 MT (prov) in 2003-04 (upto 
Feb., 04) and import of silk fabrics from 188 MT in 2000-01 to 2783 MT in 
2002-03 to 1153 MT (prov) in 2003-04 (till Sept., 04) even while prices have 
declines. This has had disruptive effect on the domestic market of silk. 
Several steps have been taken to stabilize the domestic silk industry. 
These include the following: 
(i) antidumping duty has been imposes! by Government of India with 
effect from 2nd January, 2003 on all imported malberry raw silk 
(not thrown) of international grade 2 A and below, originated in or 
exported from People's Republic of China, so as to keep the 
landed value of these goods at US$ 27.97 per kg. 
18 

[14 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) Tariff barriers to imports have been readjusted. In the Union budget 
of 8th July, 2004 the Finance Minister has declared an effective 
import tariff, including CV D and cess, on silk yarn and silk fabric 
of 30.192%. Duty on import of s ilk worm cocoon and raw silk has 
been kept at 30%. 
(iii) Several programmes and schemes to increase the quality, 
productivity and the competitiveness of the domestic silk industry 
have been instituted. The major ones are:— 
• Research and Development effo rts of Central Silk Board have 
been stepped up to improve quantity and productivity of 
sericulture, by evolution of mo re productive and stress tolerant 
breeds and hybrids of mulberry and non-mulberry food plants 
and silkworms; and development of low cost reeling and 
processing technologies in silk; 
• Seed Support and Technical Assi stance is being given by the 
Central Silk Board to State Go vernments, farmers and reelers 
by maintenance of parent races and basic seed, supply of 
commercial seed, and augmentation of grainage facilities for 
production of disease free high yielding and drought resistant 
seeds; 
• Central assistance is being extended to States through 
Centrally Sponsored & Central sector schemes to strengthen 
farm infrastructure, increase are under sericulture, upgrade 
reeling facilities, improve fini shing processes, strengthen seed 
supply cocoon and silk testing systems; 
• Low cost and productivity enhancing technologies developed 
by the Central Silk Board are being popularized through Central 
assistance to beneficiaries, training to the State' extension 
machinery and beneficiaries, organizing of various awareness 
programmes, etc.; 
• for technology upgradation of the indigenous silk industry loan 
at 5% point less than applicable bank rate, under the 
Technological Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) for the textiles 
sector is available inter alia to silk sector. 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [14 July, 2004] 
• Under the Swarnjayanti Gram Sw arojgar Yojana (SGSY) of the 
Ministry of Rural Development financial assistance is being 
provided to various States for implementation of sericulture 
projects of all varieties of silk with the technical assistance of 
CSB; 
• Supply chain issues between the farmers, raw silk producers 
and the weavers are being addr essed by advocating contract 
farming models, price linked grading, etc. 
• Establishing quality certificat ion systems for silkworm seeds, 
cocoons, yarn and fabric. 
• An amount of Rs. 450 crores has been provided in the Tenth 
Plan for the Sericulture sector to support the above strategy 
and programmes; 
• Export of value added silk items is being encouraged through 
assistance to exporters for participation in fairs and exhibitions 
abroad, market research and surveys, etc.

302. SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: Will the Minister of COAL AND 
MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the steep rise in coal prices has its 
cascading effect in prices of steel and power sector in the country; 
(b) if so, whether it is a fact that the beneficiary common man is 
severely affected by the rise in prices of prime grade coal; and

and power industry to reconsider the decision?

cost of generation of 1 unit of elec tricity and presuming the average price 
of steel as Rs. 25,500/- per tonne, the impact on steel would be less than 2%.

Assistance under NCCF for Andhra Pradesh 
334. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government of Andhra Pradesh has requested for 
early release of case assistance and rice from the National Calamity 
Contingency Fund for the December, 2003 cyclone; and 
(b) if so, the action taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI S. REGHUPATHY): (a) and (b) As per the existing scheme for 
financing relief expenditure, the State Go vernments are primarily responsible 
for undertaking relief and rehabilitation measures in the areas affected by 
natural calamities. The Government of India supplements the efforts of the 
State Governments by providing financial and logistic support, where 
necessary. 
Assistance for relief and rehabilitation in the wake of natural calamities 
is provided under two Schemes. A Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) has been 
constituted for each State. The Govern ment of India c ontributes 75% of 
the corpus of the CRF. The State Governments contribute 25%. The State 
Governments are required to meet t he expenditure for providing immediate 
relief to the victims of natural calamities from the CRF. A Committee under 
Chairmanship of the Chief Secretary of the State has been authorized 
under the Scheme of CRF to decide on  all matters connected with the 
financing of the relief expenditure. 
Where funds available in the CRF do not prove to be sufficient for 
meeting the expenditure on relief and rehab ilitation, in case a calamity of 
severe nature, financial assistance is also provided to the States from the 
National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF) in accordance with the laid 
down procedure. 
The Government of Andhra Pradesh had submitted a memorandum 
seeking financial assistance from NCC F and foodgrains in the wake of 
cyclone in December, 2003. A Central Team was deputed by the Ministry 
of Home Affairs to assess the situ ation and requirement s of funds. The 
report of the Central Team was considered by the Inter-Ministerial Group 
(IMG). The request of the State Govern ment along with the report of the 
Central Team and recommendations of the IMG thereon was to be placed 
before the High Level Committee for co nsideration and approval. However, 
in the meantime the High Level Committe e was required to be re-constituted 
after the change of the Government at the Centre. The meeting of the 
55

re-constituted Committee has now be en convened on 14th July, 2004 to 
consider the request of drought and flood/cyclone affected States including 
the State of Andhra Pradesh for cyclone of December, 2003.

the expenditure on relief operations in  the wake of cyclone of December, 
2003, out of the funds available in t he CRF. It may be stat ed that the State 
of Andhra Pradesh was allocated an amount of Rs. 229.28 crore in the 
CRF for the year 2003-04 consisting of  Rs. 171.96 crore as Central share 
and Rs. 57.32 crore as State's share.

367. SHRI DATTA MEGHE: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) the State-wise details of the number of unelectrified villages to 
be electrified in the country; 
91 

RAJYA SABHA [14 July, 2004] 
(b) whether at present a village is considered to be electrified even 
if one household in the village has access to power; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether Government propose to redefine the term 'village 
electrification' to provide for wider coverage of village households; 
(e) if so, the details thereof; 
(f) whether the Government have drawn any schedule for rural 
electrification; and 
(g) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) State-wise 
details of un-electrified villages are enclosed as Statement. (See below) 
(b) to (e) As per the old definition "a village will be deemed to be 
electrified if the electric ity is used in the inhabited locality, within the 
revenue boundary of the village, for any purpose whatsoever". 
A new definition has come into force w.e.f. 2004-05. According to 
the new definition. 
A village would be declared as electrified if 
(i) Basic infrastructure such as Distribution Transformer and 
distribution lines are provided in the inhabited locality as well as 
the Dalit Basti/hamlet where it ex ists, (for electrification through 
Non-Conventional Energy Sources a Distribution Transformer 
may not be necessary); 
 
(ii) Electricity is provided to pub lic places like Schools, Panchayat 
Office, Health Centres, Dispensarie s, Community centres etc.; and 
 
(iii) The number of households elec trified should be at least 10% of 
the total number of households in the village, 
(f) and (g) According to the National Common Minimum Programme 
household electrification is to be completed in five years. 
For achieving this target, the rural electrification strategy has been 
drawn up, which envisages: 
(i) Creation of Rural Electricity Distribution Backbone (REDB) of 
33/11 KV substations, with at least one such substation in each 
block appropriately networked and linked to the State 
transmission system, 
 
(ii) Creation of Village Electricity Infrastructure ( VEI) by providing 
Distribution Transformer(s) with at least one such transformer 
in every village. 
92 

[14 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA

368. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister 
of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) by when Government propose to announce the National 
Electricity Policy and Rural Electricity Policy;

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P. M. SAYEED) : (a) and (b) 
The Central Government is in consultation with the States formulating 
National Electricity Policy, National Policy on stand alone systems for 
rural areas and non-conventional energy system and National Policy on 
electrification and local distributions in rural areas as required under the 
electricity Act, 2003.

State Electricity Regulatory Commissions have the powers to fix tariff for

Commissions (SERCs), the State Govern ment shall pay to the concerned 
utility/licensees the full amount requi red to compensate the grant of 
subsidy.

a matter exclusively in the domain of the State Government and the Central 
Government has no role whatsoever, in this regard.

Statement 
The extracts from the supplementary report of the steering group on 
growth and investment in textiles 
6. Debt Restructuring Scheme 
6.1 The international interest rates are very low at present. Whereas 
the cotton textile industry is faced with high cost of capital duty loans 
availed prior to introduction of Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme, 
which carried the then prevailing high rates of interest. In order to enable 
Indian textile industry to compete in the global market, Government of 
India should set up a reconstruction fund with the objective of reducing 
cost of capital of existing textile units in the organised sector. It is estimated 
that the total exposure of the FIs to the textile sector in the form of term 
loan is in the region of Rs. 16000 crores, of this amount 1/3 is unlikely to 
be revived and may not be eligible for assistance. Thus, the total debt 
exposure that needs to be addressed is estimated to be about Rs. 10,000 
crores.The efforts under the restructured scheme will be to bring down 
the ultimate rate of interest to borrowers to around 8%. The aim of the 
reconstruction will be to restructure industry's existing high cost loans 
tied up in the past. 
6.2 It is recommended that: 
 
• All existing secured loans, excess drawing of working capital 
(which would be converted into working capital term loan) would 
be eligible to be covered under the fund. 
• As part of restructuring exercise, Fls/banks would reduce rate 
of interest on their existing secured loans to a threshold level of 
12% per annum. If the existing rates are lower, they would be 
maintained at that level. 
• The rate of interest on working capital would be brought down 
to PLR. 
• The Fls/banks shall waive all penal interest, liquidated damages 
etc. 
• Over due interest would be funded and converted into "zero 
121 

RAJYA SABHA [14 July, 2004] 
coupon debentures" to be repaid after liquidating the restructured 
loans along with interest. 
• An incentive of maximum 4% would be extended on the rate of 
interest leading to the final intere st cost to the textile units on 
term borrowings at 8% per annum. 
• The textile units would pay interest at the rate of 8%. Interest 
incidence upto 4% would be compensated to Fls/banks out of 
the proposed fund. 
• The loans covered under TUFS and External Commercial 
Borrowings would not be eligible under the scheme. 
• The restructured loans alongwith 8% interest would be repaid in 
a maximum period of 10 years including 2 years moratorium. 
After 10 years period no interest incentive would be extended to 
any unit. 
 
6.3 The liabilities eligible for restructuring would include secured 
liabilities and excess working capital on the cut off date. 
6.4 The scheme would remain open for two year from the date of 
announcement. Loan given during these two year period shall not be 
eligible under the scheme. Any fresh loan for modernisation and expansion 
would be eligible for interest relief under TUFS. 
6.5 The initial size of the recons truction fund will be Rs. 500 crores. 
Additional requirement of fund could be assessed on the pace and 
success of the scheme.

Action on representation by Indian Cotton Mills Federation 
392. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of TEXTILE 
be pleased to refer to reply to Unstarred Question 1686 given in the 
Rajya Sabha on 17th December, 2003 and state the action taken by the 
Ministry on the representation rece ived from the Indian Cotton Mills 
Federation? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): 
As per the Budget 2004-05 presented in the Parliament on 8.7.04, the 
duty structure of textiles has been completely revised. The CENVAT 
Scheme for textiles has been made optional and there will be mandatory 
duty only on man-made fibres/yarns {i.e., 24% on Polyester Filament 
Yarn (PFY) including textured yarn and 16% on all other filament yarns 
and man-made fibres). Except for thes e duties other textile goods will be 
fully exempt if no credit of duties is  taken under the CENVAT Credit Ruels. 
For those opting to pay the duty and thereby avail of duty credit, the 
applicable rates of duty will be 4% for pure cotton textile items (i.e., yarn, 
fabrics, garments and made-ups) and 8% for other textile items including 
yarn, fabrics, garments, and made-ups. Besides, Additional Duty on Textile 
and Textile Articles (AT & T) and Additional Excise Duty in lieu of Sales 
Tax for goods of special importance have been abolished. 
Steps for smooth running of Textile Industry 
†393. SHRI ISAM SINGH: Will the Mi nister of TEXTILES be pleased 
to state: 
(a) the number of textile industries closed in India; and 
† Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi. 
124 

[14 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) how Government propose to ensure smooth running to textile 
industry? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): 
(a) As per the information obtaine  from the Office of the Textile 
Commissioner, Mumbai, 472 cotton/man-made fibre textile mills (Non- 
SSI) (378 spinning and 94 composite mills) were lying closed in the country 
as on 31.05.04. 
(b) The Government seeks to foster a policy regime, which facilitates 
growth and development of Indian industry. It has taken a number of 
steps for revival of sick industrial units which, inter-alia, include, guidelines 
of the Reserve Bank of India to banks, amalgamation of sick units with 
healthy units, setting up of B oard for Industrial and Financial 
Reconstruction (BIFR) under the Sick Industrial Companies (Special 
Provisions) Act, etc. The Reserve Bank of India has been issuing from 
time to time elaborate guidelines covering all areas of industrial 
rehabilitation viz. detection of industrial sickness at incipient stage, 
identification of sick/weak units, carr ying out viability study of the units 
then extending relief and concessions to only viable units, co-ordination 
among banks and financial institutions  and banks themselves, norms for 
promotor's contribution, extended period for repayment/rescheduling of 
loans, conversions and waiver of penal rate/compound interest, etc. 
Taking note of challenges posed by changing global economic 
environment, the Government announced the National Textile Policy in 
November 2000 and has taken various initiatives to strengthen and to 
ensure smooth running of the Indian textile industry. Some of the important 
initiatives taken include: 
(i) Rationalisation of fiscal duty structure so as to attract investment 
and modernisation. 
(ii) Launching of the Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) 
to facilitate the modernisation and upgradation of the sector; 
(iii) For accelerating modernization of the powerlooms segment of 
the textile industry, 20% Capital assistance is available on 
investment in TUFS compatible specified machinery subject to 
a ceiling of Rs. 12 lakh on amount of assistance; 
(iv) Annoncement of a package for restructuring of debt portfolios 
125 

 
RAJYA SABHA [14 July, 2004] 
of potentially viable textile units having debt exposure of Rs 2 
crore and above; 
(v) Dereservation of the wove n segment of readymade garment 
from the SSI sector. The SSI inve stment limit for knitted/hosiery 
segment increased from Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 5 crore. 
( vi) With a view to making textile production competitive, the custom 
duty on various capital goods brought down from 25% to 5%; 
(vii) A centrally sponsored scheme titled "Apparel Park for Export 
Scheme" launched for imparting focused thrust for setting up of 
apparel manufacturing units of  international standards at 
potential growth centres and to give fillip to exports; 
(viii) For upgrading infrastructure facilities at important textile centres, 
a scheme "Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme" 
(TCIDS) has also been launched; 
(ix) Cotton Technology Mission launched to improve the productivity 
and quality of cotton; 
(x) Imposition of a combination of ad-valorem and specific duty on 
"whichever is higher basis" on import a number of textile items 
to safeguard the interest of domestic industry; 
(xi) The facility of accelerated depreciation at the rate of 50% 
extended to weaving, processing and garment machinery, which 
are covered under TUFS. Cost of machinery has also been 
reduced through reduction in customs duty and abolition of excise 
duty on certain specified machinery items; 
(xii) For boosting exports of textile and clothing Government provides 
financial assistance to Textile Export Promotion Councils under 
Marketing Development Assistance (MDA) Scheme; 
(xiii) Close monitoring of imports on regular basis so as to ensure 
that imports do not cause any seri ous detriment or injury to the 
domestic industry. In case any unfair trade practices come to the 
notice, action, if necessary, under WTO provisions are taken; 
(xiv) National Institute for Fashion Technology (NIFT), its six branches 
and Apparel Training and Design Centres (ATDC) are running 
various courses/programmes to meet skilled manpower 
126 

[14 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
requirements of textile industry especially apparel in the field of 
design, merchandising and marketing; 
(xv) Facilities by way of eco-test ing laboratories have been created 
to enable exporters to get the garments/textiles pre-tested for 
conforming to the requirements of importing countries; 
(xvi) 100% Foreign Direct Investment permitted through automatic 
route in the textile sector with certain exceptions; and 
(xvii) Refund of taxes and duties on exports through drawback route.

Incidents of suicide by farmers in various parts of the country and remedial 
measures taken by Government with regard thereto 
SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA (Jharkhand): Sir, I beg to call the attention 
of. the Minister of Agriculture on the incidents of suicide by farmers in 
various parts of the country, and remedial measures taken by the 
Government with regard thereto. 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI PRIYARANJAN  
DASMUNSI): Sir, the cases of suicide by farmers have been reported from 
the States of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Orissa, Maharashtra, Punjab, 
Rajasthan and Tripura. The number of cases of suicide has been significant 
in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Orissa and Maharashtra in the recent period 
as reported. However, the Government of Orissa has clarified that the 
cases of suicide by farmers in this State were not due to causes related to 
agriculture. The main causes as reported by the State Governments for 
committing suicide by farmers are crop failure, indebtedness, high rate of 
interest on loans, dro ught, social and economic  insecurity, incurable 
ailments, addiction to alcohol and family disputes. 
In order to tackle the problems of the farmers, the Common Minimum 
programme of the Government of UPA has identified areas requiring 
focussed and priority attention. Some of the important action points are, 
doubling rural credit in three years, easing the burden of debt, high interest 
rate and nursing cooperative banks to health, dry land farming, development 
of horticulture, improvement of water management and protection to farmers 
from imports and falling international prices. 
In order to achieve these objectives, the Finance Minister in his Budget 
Speech has announced a number of initiatives to provide relief to the 
farmers. Notable among them are, accelerating the completion of irrigation 
projects, investing in rural infrastructure, providing farm insurance and 
livestock insurance, improving agric ulture product markets and promoting 
agri-businesses and appointment of a Task Force on reforms in the 
cooperative banking system. 
ft is proposed to undertake restruct uring of debt of the farmers by 
the commercial banks, Regional Rural Banks and cooperatives. Debts 
of farmers in distress will be rescheduled /restructured in districts declared 
as calamity affected by the State Government with longer repayment 
period at current interest rates including an initial moratorium of two years. 
Farmers in arrears will receive the benefit of rescheduling of loans in

default to enable them to become eligible for fresh credit. The system of 
one-time settlement for defaulting small and marginal farmers will be put 
into operation. 
The Central Government has taken up various schemes and 
programmes for enhancing production of agriculture and horticulture crops 
like Macro-Management Scheme, Technology Mission on Horticulture in 
the North-East including Sikkim, Uttaranchal, Jammu and Kashmir, 
Integrated Scheme of Oilseeds, Pulses, Oil palm and Maize, Technology 
Mission on Cotton, Technology Mission on Coconut and On Farm Water 
Management in Eastern India. T he farmers are receiving financial 
assistance under different schemes. The Government has also provided 
safety nets in the form of National Agriculture Insurance Scheme (NAIS), 
Farmers Income Insurance Scheme (FIIS) against production loss and 
Minimum Support Price (MSP) and Market Intervention Scheme (MIS) 
against decline in prices. 
The drought relief assistance is given to the States both in the form 
of financial assistance and foodgrains as and when necessary. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI DINESH TRIVEDI) in the Chair] 
Since August, 2003, Andhra Pradesh has received Rs. 140.86 crores 
and 7.2 lakh MTs of foodgrains, Kar nataka Rs. 332.15 crores and 7.29 
lakh MTs of foodgrains and Kerala Rs. 30.65 crores and 0.61 lakh MTs of 
foodgrains. 
State Governments also provide re lief to the affected families. 
Government of Andhra Pradesh have decided to provided financial 
assistance, i.e., an ex gratia of Rs. 1 lakh to the family/next of kin of the 
deceased farmers as economic support besides loan settlement up to a 
ceiling of Rs. 50,000 as one-time settlement to creditors, each family is 
given a house under Indira Awas Yojana, admission to wards in Social 
Welfare Residential Schools Hostels.  In Karnataka, compensation of 
Rs. 110.22 lakhs to affected families of the farmers has been given. The 
interest on short-term loan has been waived and a rebate of 5.5 per cent 
is allowed on medium-term loan. Furthe r, fertilizers and seeds are supplied 
at subsidised rates. In Maharashtra, the heirs of the deceased were given 
assistance of Rs. 1 lakh from the Chief Minister's Relief Fund. 
The Government is fully conscious of the hardships of the farmers 
and will spare no efforts to solve their problems. Thank You.

SHRI RAVULA CHANDRASEKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I 
am aware of the limitations in a Calling Attention Motion. 
Sir, right from the day one, we were trying to raise the issues 
concerning the farmers. At last, Mr. Chairman is kind enough to allow us 
to raise them through this Calling Attention Motion. 
Sir, I would like to draw the attent ion of the hon. Minister towards the 
incidents o suicide by farmers in A ndhra Pradesh, the mo ratorium and its 
effects, the release of water from Karnataka, the problems concerning 
crop insurance or loan insurance, and also towards the memorandum 
submitted to the hon. Prime Minister on 1st July, 2004 in Andhra Pradesh. 
Sir, as regards the first issue of suicide committed by the farmers 
in Andhra Pradesh, as of now, for the past two months, 691 have committed 
suicide in Andhra Pradesh. Sir, I am having all the details, village-wise 
and person-wise. Even today, it appeared in the newspaper that yesterday, 
8 persons had committed suicide in Andhra Pradesh. 
The situation is alarming. It is not a blame game. I would like to 
draw the attention of the hon. Mini ster to the steps taken by the 
Government of Andhra Pradesh in t he recent past. One aspect is that 
they have declared a moratorium. On the one hand, they have declared a

moratorium for six months on private loans, excluding the loans by 
cooperative banks and commercial banks, and on the other hand, they 
are controlling the privat e money-lenders. Their action plan for the present 
year shows that the farmers ne ed Rs. 36,000 croes, whereas the 
cooperative banks and the commercial banks have come forward with an 
action plan of Rs. 11,000 crores. The farmers are at a loss to understand the 
position of the Government. From where can they get the balance amount 
of Rs. 25,000 crores for investing in the current year? The hon. Minister 
needs to pay attention to this. He should enlighten us on this. There is no 
alternative credit plan with the Government of Andhra Pradesh. I request the 
hon. Minister of the Government of India, at least to advise the Government 
of Andhra Pradesh and help them in preventing suicide of famers. 
The second aspect is regarding the release of water from Karnataka. 
We have been trying since long to im press upon the Government of India 
and the Ministry of Water Resources to see that suitable directions are 
given to Karnataka to release some water to the lower riparian State of 
Andhra Pradesh. We are having severe drinking water problem. We are 
having problems in getting water not only for agriculture but also for drinking. 
The Almatti dam is full and even today they are not releasing the water. 
Andhra Pradesh is a lower riparian State. All the dams constructed on 
Krishna river, right from Jurala, Sr isailam, Nagarjunasagar to Prakasam 
barrage, are empty. So, I urge upon the hon. Minister to see that some 
water is released to Andhra Pradesh at once, not three or four or five days 
after. The situation is alarming.

issue at all; nor is it an occasion for blaming Government 'A' or Government

issue, a social issue that requires to be dealt with by other measures than 
merely by this kind of political criticism. Sir, looking at the Budget, there 
is no doubt that the Finance Minister has done his best to create measures 
and make allocations, which doubtlessly will solve the problems of the 
farmers. But the benefits which will  accrue to the farmers from the 
implementation of the Budget are going to be long-ranging benefits and 
which are not going to percolate down immediately to the farmers' level 
and those who are on the verge of terminating their life. And if there are 
people who are bent on committing suicide now, I do not think they can

adequate familiarity with agriculture and the problems of agriculture, I am

conference of the hon. Members both in Assemblies and in Parliament 
who represent the farmer lobby, who can really speak on behalf of the

Need to Withdraw the Move to Tax NRI Deposits 
SHRI M . P. ABDUSSAMAD SAMADANI (Kerala): Sir, through your 
respected self, I request the hon. Financ e Minister and the Government to 
withdraw the decision in the Budget to  tax non-resident, external deposits. 
This move is going to affect the life of a large number of NRIs, especially 
those, who have gone to countries like those in the Gulf region for livelihood. 
Most of them belong to the poor and middle classes, who find it very 
difficult to get a job in their motherland. They deposit their income in the 
banks, so as to use it for their family's basic needs like construction of a 
house, or, the marriage of a daughter. 
Sir, the contribution of NRIs to the Indian economy is laudable. In 
certain States like Kerala, it forms the backbone of the economy, and a 
large number of families depend on it. 42 per cent of the deposits in the 
banks of Kerala are contributed by t he NRIs. The move to tax NRI deposits 
is going to affect the banking system of Kerala badly. It will be a burden for 
a large number of job seekers who go abroad, compelled by non- 
employment. The Banks of Kerala have already expressed their anxiety. 
The Chief Minister of Kerala and various political parties have asked the 
Government to withdraw the move. 
Sir, it is regrettable and deplorabl e that the Budget, which has made 
various tax concessions, has created ne w hurdles in the way of NRIs, who 
are the real ambassadors of our count ry. They deserve our Government's 
assistance. I request the hon. finance Mini ster to withdraw the decision at 
the earliest, and to remove the anxiety of our NRIs.

SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the State of 
Andhra Pradesh has got the oldest delta s. The soils being heavy in these 
areas, the State is facing severe problem of water logging and impeded 
drainage. An estimated area of about 1.1 m hectare suffers from drainage

have sprung up in the coastal area, converting fertile rice fields (about 
50,000 hectare) for this purpose obstructing free flow of drainage water 
during times of heavy rains and floods. This has added new dimension to 
the chronic problem of drainage in t he coast. The State of Andhra Pradesh 
is one of the prosperous agricultural States of India, significantly contributing 
to the production of foodgrains, oilseeds and commercial crops. The 
production and productivity of crops will be further enhanced in this State 
if due attention is paid to the drai nage improvement. It is understood that 
the State has not been included in the National Drainage Technology 
Programme, contemplated by the Union Government.

Andhra Pradesh in the National Drainage Technology Programme for under- 
taking research as well as for trials, demonstrations for large scale adoption 
of drainage improvement measures in the common areas of the State.

Need to Legislate to Protect the Lower Riparian States 
SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I wish to impress upon 
the need for bringing a suitable legislation as envisaged in Entry 56 of the 
Union List given in the Constitution, to protect the interests of lower riparian 
States. The inter-State river water di sputes adjudication under the Inter- 
State Water Disputes Act of 1956, does  not provide timely help to the 
suffering States. The Cauvery water dispute is a glaring example. The 
Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal was set up in June, 1990, and an interim 
award was given on 25th June, 1991. Af ter persistent effort by the hon. 
Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, the interim award was gazetted by the Union 
Government on 11th December, 1991. Ev en that did not bring solace to 
Tamil Nadu. After 14 years of anxious wait, justice is still not in sight. 
Same is the fate of all the riparian States of 14 major and 9 medium inter- 
State rivers. Anticipating such situ ations, our constitution-makers have 
provided ample power to the Union under Entry 56 of List 1 to legislate for 
the regulation and development of inter-State rivers and river valleys. Time 
has come for the Centre to act in this direction. Such a step by the Union 
will have the advantage of ensuring a quick solution to such disputes. This 
will also take care of the voices of dissent raised against the linking of 
major rivers in the country. So, I appeal to the Government to bring a 
comprehensive legislation under Entry 56 of List 1 and safeguard the 
interests of lower riparian States.

you, Sir, to the Government to have  the matter examined and send Central 
assistance urgently before people in the nearby areas also get affected,

protects their basic rights and as such it is the duty of the Government to 
honour the same. Thank you.

Need for Early Completion of Doordarshan Transmitter Work and 
Enhancement of Radio Station at Dharmupuri, Tamil Nadu 
SHRI C. PERUMAL (TAMIL NADU): Sir, Dharmapuri is a backward 
district in Tamil Nadu, it has no ma jor industry. Two years ago, a full- 
fledged radio station was set up at Dharmapuri. The radio station was 
constructed at a cost of  Rs. 4.03 crores. All the infrastructural facilities 
have been completed and the station is ready for operations. 
At present, the statio n has a 3 KW capacity and can be heard up to 
40 Kms. distance. However, the stat ion has the capacity and potential to 
function with 10 KW which can be heard beyond a distance of 60 Kms. 
The station has an independent studio and other facilities required for a 
separate station. However, the ra dio station has not commenced its 
operations. It is understood that the necessary staff have not been provided 
and that is why it has not commenc ed its operations. I demand that 
necessary staff should be posted immediately so that the radio station 
commences its operations. Otherwise, all the money and labour would 
become a waste. 
It is also understood that a High Power Transmitter for Doordarshan 
is being set up at Dharmapuri. However, the work is progressing at a slow 
pace. I demand that the work should be completed on a top priority by 
allocating adequate funds. Moreover, ev en smaller districts have FM radio 
stations. Dharmapuri is a large district and if an FM channel is provided,

Need to Exempt Customs Duty on Raw Material Imported for 
Manufacture of Micro Irrigation System in Andhra Pradesh 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDI SIRIGIREDDY (ANDHRA PRADESH): 
Sir, the State of A ndhra Pradesh is the "Rice Bowl " of the country, but it is 
facing acute shortage of water over the last three to four years and this is 
severely hampering the agricultural acti vity in the State. In Andhra Pradesh 
State, agriculture contributes 30 per  cent to the State's GSDP. The 
sustainability of this vital economic ac tivity for 60 per cent of the State 
population is severely undermined due to the dwindling of groundwater 
resources and misuse of surface water. The Government of Andhra Pradesh 
is planning to launch a Micro Irrigation Project to achieve sustainable 
growth in agriculture and for an effective management of water, with a 
project outlay of Rs. 1,200 crores, cove ring an area of 2.5 lakh hectares in 
two years. The aim of the project is to take the benefits of micro irrigation 
to the agricultural field of every farmer in Andhra Pradesh. The Government 
of Andhra Pradesh is giving a subsidy of  50 per cent on every micro irrigation 
unit to every eligible farmer. In spite of this subsidy, the Micro Irrigation 
Systems are fairly capital-intensive. 
So, to reduce the cost of micro irrigation equipment, the Government of 
Andhra Pradesh has already exempted Sales Tax and the Union Govemment 
too has exempted the Central Excise Duty. But, to make the equipment more 
affordable to the farmer, I request the Fi nance Minister to exempt the Customs 
Duty to be levied on raw material that is used in the production of Micro 
Irrigation System. The exemption would bring down the pric e of the equipment 
by 50 per cent which helps the farmer in getting higher crop. 
Matter Raised with Permission—contd.

Progress of construction work of NH-57 
† *142. PROF. RAM DEO BHANDARY: Will the Minister of 
ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) the progress of construction work of National Highway No. 57 
in Bihar; 
(b) the amount spent on the wi dening and strengthening of the 
said highway during the last three years; 
(c) whether the said project would be completed within the stipulated 
period; and 
(d) if so, Government's plan in this regard, year-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS: 
(SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) to (d) National Highway No. 57 from km 0.00 to km 
310.00 in Bihar is proposed to be four laned as part of East-West corridor 
under Phase-ll of the National Highways Development Project (NHDP). 
The Detailed Project Report is under preparation. The civil works are targeted 
for award by March 2005 and completed by December 2007, within the 
stipulated target for completion of four laning of East-West corridor. 
No amount has been spent on civil works for four laning of NH-57 
in the last three years. However, Rs. 34.79 crore has been spent on 
improvement and maintenance of NH-57 in the last three years.

Task force on problems of WLL vs. GSM 
*147. SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
Will the Minister of COMM UNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have constituted a Task Force of technical 
experts from NTs, CSIR, TCIL and others to ensure that WLL Limited 
mobile services do not suffer due to unnecessary representation by 
Cellular Operators Association of India; and 
18 

[15 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details of the outcome of the Task Force constituted to 
look into the problems of WLL vs. GSM? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI DAYANIDHI MARAN): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The 
Government constituted a Task Force of technical experts from Telecom 
Regulatory Authority of India, Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur and 
Council for Scientific and Industrial Research on 3rd October, 2003 to: 
(i) identify modalities for restricting Limited Mobility Service to Short 
Distance Charging Area (SDCA) on Wireless Local Loop (WLL) 
platform and enforcing all other parameters laid down by the 
Licensor; 
(ii) to go into the issue of technology including interface architecture, 
software engineering between the Cellular Mobile Service and 
Limited Mobility Service provided by Basic Service Operators apart 
from examining any relevant issue. 
The Task Force submitted its repo rt to the Government on 27th 
November, 2003. 
The Task Force had come to a conclusion that Software 
Management practices deployed by various operators could be adequate 
to ensure Mobility Management as per the licensing requirements 
provided multiple registration practice i.e. the authentication of same 
wireless terminal in more than one SDCA is not permitted. All Base 
stations in a particular SDCA can be grouped in a unique User Zone 
Identification i.e. switch database identifies a group consisting of a set 
of Base Trans-receiver Stations (B TSs) physically located in a given 
SDCA. Subscriber from a given SDCA should be subscribed to one and 
only one User Zone Identification i.e. the one associated with the home 
SDCA where subscriber is actually registered. System Identification Code 
(ID) (used in entire network in Circ les), Network ID (used in switch 
database to identify a network or a part of network) and User Zone ID 
can be effectively used to restrict mobility within the SDCA. 
The Government accepted the Report of the Task Force and accordingly 
instructions were issued to Basic Service Licensees as well as Unified Access 
Service Licensees migrated from Basic Services on 4th February, 2004.

Relations with Pakistan and Bangladesh 
*149. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the extent of progress made in developing relations with Pakistan 
and Bangladesh in socio-economic and political fields; 
(b) whether the issue of trade and commerce from the North- 
Eastern region with Bangladesh and with other regions of our country 
across Bangladesh has been taken up so far; and 
(c) the achievements in this respect so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) to (c) Government is committed to 
the development of peaceful, fri endly and cooperative relations with 
Pakistan. Several significant steps have been taken to normalise 
diplomatic and other links, and promote people to people contacts. In 
this context, there have been exchanges at the level of Parliamentarians, 
jurists, journalists, sportsmen, artistes, businessmen, etc. Prisoners and 
fishermen have been released on both sides, and the visits by pilgrim 
groups resumed. In addition, a ceasefire along the International Border, 
Line of Control and the Actual Ground Position Line (AGPL) in Jammu 
20 

[15 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
and Kashmir has been in effect from the midnight of November 25,2003. 
In the Joint Press Statement of January 6, 2004, President Musharraf 
reassured the Prime Minister of India that he will not permit any territory 
under Pakistan's control to be used to support terrorism in any manner 
The Foreign Secretaries of the two countries met on February 18, 2004 
to commence the process of the Composite Dialogue. The ongoing 
process of confidence building and dialogue with Pakistan has been 
taken forward and intensified. External Affairs Minister met Foreign 
Minister Kasuri of Pakistan on a couple of occasions and they reviewed 
progress on all aspects of bilateral relations. There have been positive 
interactions between the drug control authorities of the two countries, 
and BSF and Pakistan Rangers. The Expert level Dialogue on Nuclear 
CBMs on June 19-20 resulted in several measures to enhance 
communication links, and working for confidence building measures such 
as Agreement on pre-notification of flight testing of missiles. The Foreign 
Secretaries of India and Pakistan met on 27-28 June, 2004. Recalling 
the reassurance contained in the Jo int Press Statement of January 6, 
2004, they exchanged views on carry ing the process forward in an 
atmosphere free from terrorism and violence. The two sides proposed a 
comprehensive framework for convent ional CBMs aimed at initiating 
and enhancing communication, coordination and interaction. They 
agreed, inter alia, to restore the strength of respective high commissions 
to the original level of 110, and release all apprehanded fishermen. It 
was also agreed to schedule the meetings of the remaining six subjects 
of the Composite Dialogue on Siachen, Wullar Barrage/Tulbul Navigation 
Project, Sir Creek, Terrorism and Drug Trafficking, Economic and 
Commercial Cooperation and Promotion of Friendly Exchanges in various 
fields, between the third week of July and the first half of August, 2004. 
2. Relations with Bangladesh have expended in recent years, including 
in the socio-economic and political fields. High-level exchanges, including 
regular formal and informal consultations between the Foreign Ministers, 
characterise the relationship. Meetings of the Ministerial level Joint Economic 
Commission and the Joint Revers Commission are held periodically. Other 
structured bilateral interactions include those between the Foreign Secretaries, 
the Home Secretaries, the Commerce Secretaries, the BSF and the BDR. 
There are allso Joint Working Groups between the Home Ministries, on trade 
and on customs cooperation. Cooperation on cultural and academic matters 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [15 July, 2004] 
are covered by a bilateral agreement. A revised bilateral visa agreement was 
signed in 2001. As a result of these exchanges and other initiatives to promote 
bilateral ties, there has been a greater degree of trust and mutual understanding 
on political matters and significant increase in trade, in people to people 
contacts and in cultural exchanges between the two countries. 
3. The Government is committed to promoting increased trade and 
commerce between the North Eastern Region and Bangladesh and other 
parts of the country and has raised the issue of grant of transit for Indian 
goods through Bangladesh with the Government of Bangladesh at 
various levels. Bangladesh has not agreed to grant of these transit 
facilities over land, though transit through inland waterways takes place 
in accordance with a bilateral protocol signed in this regard.

*161. SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH  SHARMAH: Will the PRIME

(b) if so, the percentage of people living below the poverty line, as

proposed to be formulated; and

(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) The ranking of States by the per 
capita State Domestic Product (SDP) indicates that Assam is one of the 
poorest States in the country. Among the major States, Bihar and Uttar 
Pradesh had lower per capita SDP in 2001-02, the last year for which 
data is available. The National Human Development Report, 2001 
indicates that amongst major States, Bihar has a lower Human 
Development Index (HDI) than Assam in 2001.

line (1999-2000 estimates). As per census data 2001, percentage of literate 
persons in the State is 64.28. Percentage of drop-out rates from Class-I

Category State, entitling the State to receive funds for their

and communication, power, health, flood control, etc., from

least 10% of their plan budget for schemes and

have been specifically exempt ed by the Government). The 
amount remaining unspent from this 10% allocation is 
transferred to a Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources 
(NLCPR) for development in the NER. State is getting

Khadi Gramodyog in Chhattisgarh 
 
† 153. SHRI MOTILAL VORA: Will the Minister of AGRO AND 
RURAL INDUSTRIES be pleased to state:- 
(a) whether Government propose to promote Khadi Gramodyog in 
the State of Chhattisgarh; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the number of people likely to be benefited from these 
industries? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRO A ND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRI 
MAHABIR PRASAD): (a) and (b) For the development of Khadi and 
Village Industries in the country, the Government of India is already 
implementing the Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP) 
through Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) throughout 
the country including the State of Chhattisgarh. Under this scheme, 
margin money assistance is provided at the rate of 25% of the project 
cost for the projects upto Rs. 10.00 lakhs. For projects costing above 
Rs. 10.00 lakhs, and upto Rs. 25.00 lakhs, rate of Margine Money is 
25% of Rs. 10.00 lakhs, plus 10% of the remaining cost of the project. 
For weaker sections viz. SC/ST/Ex-Servicemen Women/Minority/ 
Physical Handicapped/OBC beneficiaries belongs to NE Region, Sikkim, 
Andaman Nicobar and Lakshadweep etc., the margin money grant is 
30% of the project cost upto Rs. 10 lakhs and 10% of the remaining cost 
of the project upto Rs. 25 lakhs. The scheme is being implemented 
through Public Sector Banks, RRBs, Private Sector Scheduled 
Commercial Banks etc. The borrower is required to invest a contribution 
of 10% of the project cost and in the case of weaker sections, it is 5%. 
Further, for the development of Khadi and Village Industries sector in 
the country including Chhattisgarh, the Government is implementing Rebate/ 
Scheme, Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate Scheme (ISEC) providing 
subsidized rate of interest on bank loans and Product Development Design 
Intervention and Packaging (PRODIP) scheme for improved designs. 
(c) Under the REGP scheme,  about 1131 projects have been 
financed, generating 31989 job opportunities (upto 31.03.2004) in the 
State of Chhattisgarh, since its inception in the year 2000-01. Under this 
scheme, for the year 2004-05 a target for generating 15025 job 
opportunities in the State of Chhattisgarh has been fixed.

Maiden Flight By Saras 
*154. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a 14-seater civilian passenger aircraft 
'Saras' has been indigenously dev eloped and its prototype made a 
successful flight recently at the HAL Airport, Bangalore; 
(b) if so, the distinctive feature of the aircraft; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the prototype aircraft has exceeded 
its intended weight, reducing the payload it can carry and the range; 
(d) if so, the steps being taken to achieve the desired specifications; and 
(e) the details of surveys conducted to project demand for the 
aircraft for domestic needs and the international market and plans drawn 
for its commercial production? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Yes Sir, the first prototype of 
the indigenously developed SARAS aircraft VT-XSD had its successful 
maiden test flight on 29th May 2004 at HAL airport, Bangalore. 
(b) The distincitve features of the Aircraft are as follows: 
'SARAS' is a multi-role light transport aircraft designed and developed 
by the National Aerospace Laboratories, Bangalore. It is designed to carry 
14 passengers and the first prototype is powered by two turboprop engines 
(pusher) each developing 850 shaft horsepower (SHP). The second proto 
type will be fitted with a higher power  engine of the same family (1200 
SHP), which will also be the case for the production of standard aircraft. 
SARAS is capable of cruising upto a maximum speed of about 550 km./ 
hr and upto an altitude of 30,000 ft. It has a pressurised cabin and provides 
passenger comfort similar to those provided by the regional jet airliners. It 
is capable of operating from short and semi prepared runways and in hot 
and humid climate. It has a wingspan of 14.7 m. and an overall length of 
14.63 m. The various roles considered for SARAS include commuter, 
aerial survey, air ambulance, VIP transport, light cargo transport etc. 
(c) Yes Sir, the prototype did exceed its intended weight. It is very 
common to have prototypes having higher weight than what is eventually 
achieved by refinements in desgin and fabrication in the production stage. 
In the case of SARAS, the maximum take off weight was estimated as 
35 

RAJYA SABHA  [15 July, 2004] 
6100 kg. way back in 1996. This was well before the detailed design 
was done and the actual subsystems were selected. Mechanisms are 
put in place so that specified payload and range are not affected by the 
time SARAS aircraft reaches the stage of production. 
(d) The following steps are taken to meet the desired specifications: 
(i) Reduction of the margin available in the basic structure (based 
on analysis and structural testing); 
(ii) Optimization of the struct ure based on design modifications; 
and 
(iii) Fitting with the higher power engine (1200 SHP) in the 2nd 
prototype to meet the safety standards associated with FAR 25 
requirement under single engine failure conditions. 
(e) The last survey was conduc ted by NAL in December 2001, 
based on primary and secondary surveys coupled with a macro-economic 
model. The results of this survey indicate that in the feeder aircraft role, 
there is an expected cumulative demand of about 50 aircraft by 2007- 
08. A separate survey was also carried out, as a part of this study, for the 
North Eastern region of the country, based on a development model. 
This has predicted a demand for 18 sm all aircraft in this region by the 
year 2005. In addition of the cargo,  ambulance, aerial survey, executive 
aircraft roles and military requirements are taken into account, the 
demand is expected to be 150 aircrafts in the next ten years.

loss in travelling out of USA to get their visas extended. The application

these procedures to comply with their domestic legislation.

Statement 
Details regarding the TRAI recommendations on accelerating growth 
of Internet and Broadband Penetration 
1. Definition and goals: 
■ Brodband is an "An always-on data connection that is able to 
support various interactive services, and has the capability of a 
minimum download speed of 256 Kbps." This will be revised 
upwards in the future. 
■ India can acheive 20 million broadband and 40 million internet 
subscribers by 2010, which translate to penetration levels of 
1.7% and 3.4% respectively. This is a bare minimum target and 
will need to be upgraded as progress is made. 
2. Access to the customer in the last mile: 
■ Enabling the use of the existing infrastructure on the incumbents' 
cooper to reach customers via Digital Subscriber Loop (DSL). 
■ Decreasing artificial costs in the operation of Direct to Home 
(DTH) and Very Small Aperture Terminal (VSAT) Platforms, while 
allowing broadband services to be offered via these technologies. 
■ Allowing terrestrial wireless solutions to spread more effectively 
as a means to reach customers with today's technologies, as 
well as those in the near future. 
■ Enabling right of way clearance systems to be further streamlined 
for both current and future build-out efforts. 
3. Costs of backhaul networks: 
■ Allowing customers to realize the benefits of competition in 
domestic leased lines while compensating for the current lack 
of such competition in "within city" links. 
■ Identifying the steps that need to be taken to make National 
Internet Exchange of India (NIXI) effective and attractive for 
Internet Service Providers (ISPs) of all sizes to willingly 
participate. 
59 

RAJYA SABHA [15 July, 2004] 
4. Fiscal policies: 
 Encouraging the availability of low cost access devices through 
depreciation, donation and recycling of used Personal 
Computers (PCs). 
■ Decreasing to the level of duties on mobile phones the current 
overall levels of duties for imported items used in broadband 
networks, and equalizing duties. Growth of Internet and 
Broadband on inputs and domestically manufactured goods with 
those that are imported. 
■ Providing the appropriate tax structure to enable faster growth, 
without the Government having to forego significant revenue. 
5. Creation of content and applications: 
■ Outlining how the Government should proceed in being more 
aggressive in its efforts to create content and applications 
available online for interacting with citizens, and thereby serve 
as a leading example.

Secretary level talks with Pakistan 
418. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: W ill the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Foreign Secretary level talks with Pakistan have 
been held in June this year; and 
(b) if so, the proposals and issues discussed therein? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) and (b) Foreign Secretary level 
talks between India and Pakistan were held in New Delhi on June 27- 
28, 2004. The two Foreign Secretaries discussed the subjects 'Peace 
and Security including CBMs' and 'Jammu and Kashmir' within the 
framework of the Composite Dialogue. They exchanged views on 
carrying the process forward in an atmosphere free from terrorism 
and violence. In the Joint Statement issued at the end of the talks on 
June 28, the Foreign Secretaries, inter alia, approved the measures 
recommended by the Expert level meeting on nuclear CBMs in New 
Delhi on 19-20 June, 2004. The two sides proposed a comprehensive 
framework for CBMs aimed at initiating and enhancing 
communication, coordination and interaction. It was also agreed to 
immediately restore the strength of  the respective High Commissions 
to the original level of 110; to immediately release all apprehended 
fishermen in each other's custody and put in place a mechanism for 
the return of unintentionally transgressing fishermen and their boats 
from high seas without apprehending them; and to initiate steps for 
early release of civilian prisoners. It was also agreed in principle to 
re-establish the Consulates General in karanchi and Mumbai.

Statement 
Illegal immigration to foreign countries 
During the past few years, a number of Indian Missions/Posts 
abroad have brought to Ministry's no tice several incidents of Indian 
nationals-individually or in groups-making attempts to migrate to countries 
in Western Europe and North America through illegal and fraudulent 
means. Many of these illegal immigran ts are from Punjab. They try to 
migrate illegally mainly for economic reasons and are often assisted by 
unscrupulous agents and touts to whom they pay large sums of money. 
These illegal immigrants are taken to the developed countries in Western 
Europe and North America through Russia and other Eastern European 
countries which are used as transit countries for the purpose of illegal 
immigration. The general modus operandi for such activities is that after 
leaving India they intentionally lose or destroy their travel documents to 
prevent verification of their real identity/nationality status and their 
repatriation back to India. After reaching the country of their destination 
they either apply for political asylum or refugee status on one ground or 
the other or even obtain fake/forged travel documents establishing their 
right of residence in the country destination. They make use of loopholes 
in the local legal system, including by getting married to a local person 
for the purpose of obtaining citizenship, in order to prolong their stay in 
the country of destination with t he ultimate aim of staying there 
permanently. However, many such illegal immi grants are caught and 
put in foreign jails. 
2. Illegal immigration has largely been taking place from the 
developing and least developed countries to the developed countries in 
Western Europe, North America, Australia and New Zealand. However, 
in the post-9/11 scenario European and North American countries which 
were favoured desinations for illegal immigration have made their rules 
more stringent. The result is that not only the number of persons going 
to there countires as illegal i mmigrants has come down but these 
countries have also started repatriating illegal immigrants to their home 
countries. 
3. The illegal immigration from  India continues unabated and 
various countries of the world, particularly Western Europe and North 
America as also transit countries in Eastern Europe, are swamped by 
85 

RAJYA SABHA [15 July, 2004] 
fresh illegal immigrants from India almost on a daily basis. The number 
of agents and touts also seems to be increasing as illegal immigrants try 
to use all means including illegal means, to reach their destinations. 
4. Both the Central and State Governments have been working to 
identify agents and touts involved in illegal immigration and to take all 
necessary measures against them. The Government is also cooperating 
with the foreign countries for the speedy repatriation of India illegal 
immigrants.

Expansion of game sanctuaries 
*162. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to extend the land area under 
game sanctuaries by buying up adjacent land; 
(b) whether it is a fact that ther e is a need to extend the area 
reserved for game sanctuaries; 
(c) whether any plan is under consideration of Government to help 
State Governments acquire nearby land to sanctuaries; 
(d) if so, the details of such plans; and 
(e) the States which have been selected for this purpose? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A. 
RAJA): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) There are no Game Sanctuaries, as such, in the country. 
Only four categories of Protected Areas, viz., National Parks, Sanctuaries, 
Conservation Reserves and Community  Reserves are there under the 
Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. The National Wild Life Action Plan (2002- 
2016) envisages extension of Protected Areas from nearly 4.8 percent 
at present to ten percent of the country's geographical area. This will be 
achieved mainly through the establishment of Conservation Reserves 
in Government owned lands and of Community Reserves in community 
of private lands where the community or individuals volunteer to protect 
the wild life and its habitat. 
(c) to (e) Provision has been made under the Centrally Sponsored 
schemes of Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries, Project 
Tiger and Project Elephant for relocation, rehabilitation and acquisition 
of land for resettlement of people and to ensure habitat and corridor 
development of wild animals. Financial assistance for this purpose is 
provided to the State Governments on demand driven basis and subject 
to the availability of funds.

Conversion of forest villages into revenue villages in Assam 
*175. SHRI URKHAO GWRA BR AHMA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of forest villages converted into revenue villages in 
Assam; 
(b) what is Government's policy to convert all forest villages, which 
have fulfilled the necessary criteria, into revenue villages; and 
(c) the steps, if any, to include some villages under forest village 
category which were settled before 1981 itself? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A. 
RAJA): (a) No proposal has been received from the Government of 
Assam for conversion of forest villages into revenue villages. 
(b) The Central Government have issued policy guidelines on 
18-09-1990, under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, for conversion 
of forest villages into revenue villages. According to these guidelines, 
the Central Government may convert recognised forest villages into 
revenue villages on the basis of the proposal submitted by the concerned 
State/UT Government under the said Act. The Central Government would 
consider all land on which pattas have been issued prior to 25-10-1980 
by the authorised officers and the land is in continuous possession of 
the patta holders or their legal successors. These lands will include land 
under habitation, existing buildings, gochar lands, health centre, 
community centre, cremation ground, road etc. Further, it has also been 
clarified that the State Government  shall submit a map delineating the 
external boundaries of the areas wh ere pattas have been issued pre- 
1980. It should not be necessary for them to submit details of individual 
pattas. 
(c) There is no general provision to include villages not recognised 
as forest villages into the category of  forest villages. However, according 
to the said guidelines issued on 18-09-1990, certain specific habitations 
in forest areas which are more than twenty five years old, other than 
recognised forest villages, involving sizeable group of families, may be 
examined case by case on merits for their amicable settlement on the 
43 

RAJYA SABHA [16 July, 2004] 
basis of the proposal submitted by the concerned State/UT Government 
under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. Moreover, at present, legal 
status of forest land can not be changed due to the ban imposed by the 
Supreme Court of India on dereservation of forest land vide their order 
dated 13-11-2000 in W.P. No. 337 of 1995.

†*177. SHRI HARISH RAWAT: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any national norms in respect of the availability of health 
services have been prescribed for various States; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the availa bility of health services in a 
number of States is very deplorable as compared to other States; and 
(c) if so, the details of steps being taken to improve the state of 
health services in such States, pa rticularly in far-flung backward hilly 
areas? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) Population based norms have been 
prescribed for establishment of rural healthcare institutions, namely the 
Sub Centres, Primary Health Centres and Community Health Centres 
along with their staffing pattern and the norms are different for general 
areas and the tribal and hilly areas. Such population based norms have 
also been prescribed for ur ban healthcare infrastructure viz. Urban Family 
Welfare Centres and Urban Health Posts. 
(b) Differences in availability of hea lth services have been observed 
across states in terms of both establishment of public health institutions 
and staffing of the institutions vis-a-vis the norms as also due to shortage 
of essential drugs and consumables and lack of diagnostic and treatment 
facilities. 
(c) Health is a State subject and the responsibility of improving the 
state of health services primarily rests with the State Governments. 
However, the Central Government has been making every effort to 
increase its contribution to public health expenditure. The resources for 
public investment in health sector are being augmented by securing 
assistance from various bilateral and multilateral agencies for 
implementation of various disease control programmes. For improving 
primary healthcare services, the Tenth Plan goal is to establish primary 
healthcare institutions required to meet the healthcare needs of the 1991 
population as per the norms. For meeting needs of the growing 
population, the strategy is to strengthen the established institutions 
instead of opening new institutions.

Distribution of BPL Ration Cards 
531. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS. FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether steps will be taken to measure poverty by looking 
directly at the current data on consumption; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and if not the reason therefor; 
(c) whether the below poverty line ration cards were distributed 
based on the quantities required to give 2400 calories; 
(d) if so, the total below poverty line ration cards distributed as on 
date, State-wise; and 
(e) whether steps will be taken to introduce Universal Public 
Distribution System instead of Targeted Public Distribution System? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) and (b) At pres ent, Planning Commission is using 
per capita consumption expenditure as the yard stick to assess a person 
living below the poverty line. The per capita consumption norm has been 
fixed at Rs. 49.09 per month in rural areas and Rs. 56.64 per month in 
urban areas at 1973-74 prices at national level corresponding to a basket 
of goods and service anchored on a norm of per capita calorie 
requirement of 2400 kcal in rural areas and 2100 kcal in urban areas. 
The rational poverty line at 1999-2000 prices is Rs. 327.56 per capita 
per month in rural areas and Rs. 454.11 per month in urban areas. 
(c) Under the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS), 35 kg 
of food grains per family per month is being allocated. The Public 
Distribution System is supplemental in nature and does not envisage 
meeting the full requirements of foodgrains of any person or any class 
in full. However, the enhanced allocation of foodgrains fulfils around 
50% of the cereal requirement ev ery month for an average BPL 
household. 
(d) State-wise distribution of ration cards under BPL is given in the 
Statement (See below). 
(e) At present there is no proposal to introduce Universal Public 
Distribution System instead of TPDS.

Reforms in sale management of agricultural products 
†535. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be 
pleased to state; 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is a great difference between the 
producer's cost and consumer price of the agricultural products in the 
country due to faulty management of sale of the same; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that a gap to the extent of 100 
per cent to 500 per cent in producer's cost and consumer price in a 
number of agricultural products has been found; 
(c) if so, Government's reaction in this regard; and 
(d) the measures Government are taking to make comprehensive 
reforms in the sale management of agricultural products? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): 
(a) and (b) The difference between the price received by producer and 
the consumer's price for agricultural commodities depend on various 
factors such as type of commodity, its perishability, distance from the 
consumer market, etc. Various studies conducted by the Directorate of 
Marketing and Inspection, Faridabad, an attached office of the Ministry 
of Agriculture has revealed that the producer share in consumer price 
in respect of foodgrains and oilseeds ranges from 65 to 70 per cent, 
while in case of vegetables such as potato and onion, it ranges from 
45 to 60 per cent. Recent study conducted by Confederation of Indian 
Industries has revealed that in the case of fruits and vegetables, farmer 
realizes less than 30 per cent of the final consumer price. 
(c) and (d) The agricultural marketing system in the country needs 
to be integrated and strengthened to enhance the share of farmers in 
the ultimate price of agricultural pr oduce. Towards this end, States 
have been advised to liberalize the law governing agricultural markets 
(APMC Act) to facilitate development of competitive markets by private 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
104 

[16 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
and co-operative sectors; allow pr ocurement of agricultural commodities 
directly from farmer's field and to establish effective linkage between 
the farm production and the retail chai n and Food Processing Industries. 
States have also been advised to provide institutional support to contract 
farming arrangements in which national and multi-national companies 
enter into contracts for marketing of agricultural produce as an effective 
method of linking small farmers to source of extension advice, seed, 
credit and to assured and profitable markets. At the National Conference 
of State Agriculture Minister held at New Delhi on 07.01.2004, all the 
State Governments agreed to review  their respective APMC Act for 
implementing the suggested reforms.

under the National River Conservation Plan (NRCP). The objective of

Protection to marine environment 
545. PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ : Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that United Nations chose the World 
Environment Day, 2004 to focus attention on Marine Environment; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that India's Marine Environment has 
become vulnerable; and 
(c) if so, what measures Government have taken or envisages 
to take to protect marine environment? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The marine environment throughout the world 
including India is facing challeng es. The Government of India has 
taken following steps for protection of the Marine Environment: 
* A National Committee has been constituted to advise the 
Government on policy guidelines for implementing 
programmes on conservation and management of wetlands, 
mangroves, and coral reefs. 30 mangrove areas and 4 coral 
reefs have been identified for intensive conservation and 
preparation of management action plans. 
* Coral reefs have been included in Schedule 1 of the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972. 
* All India Co-ordinated Project  on Coastal and Marine Bio- 
diversity launched during the year 1999-2000 envisages 
Survey and Inventorisation, Training and Capacity Building in 
Taxonomy and Establishment of Database Network. 
* A notification was issued in 1991 under the Environment 
(Protection) Act, 1986, regulating developmental activities in 
coastal areas falling in the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ). 
As per this notification, all the coastal States/Union Territories 
have prepared Coastal Zone Management Plans and are 
114 

[16 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
required to regulate development activities as per the 
provisions of this notification as amended from time to time. 
* Coastal Zone Management Authorities (CZMAs) have been 
constituted in all the coastal States/Union Territories to ensure 
implementation of the provisions of the CRZ Notification, 
1991. Similarly, National Coastal Zone Management Authority 
has been constituted to develop guidelines and review the 
progress of implementation of CRZ Notification, 1991. 
* A national contingency plan to deal with oil spill disasters has 
been prepared. India has ratified Marpol 73/78 and adopted 
the provisions in the Merchant Shipping Act. 
* The concept of Integrated Coastal and Marine Area 
Management (ICMAM) Programme has been launched to 
ensure the sustainable development of the coastal areas, 
rational utilization of marine resources, and proper 
management of the marine environment to prevent its 
degradation from developmental, commercial, or other 
activities. 
* The Coastal Shelterbelt Plantation Projects under Integrated 
Afforestation and Eco-development Project Scheme (IAEPS) 
envisage plantation in rows along the coastline to create a 
shelterbelt for checking soil erosion and sand ingress for 
protection of agricultural fields, roads etc. 
* Sunderbans in West Bengal, Gulf of Mannar in Tamil Nadu 
and Nicobar Islands have been designated as Biosphere 
Reserves. 
* The coastal stretches which are subjected to the pollution 
have been identified under Co astal Ocean Monitoring and 
Prediction System (COMAPS) study conducted by the 
Department of Ocean Development in the States of Gujarat, 
Maharashtra, Goa, Pondicherry, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, 
Tamil Nadu, Orissa and West Bengal and Government of 
India has stipulated limits for discharge of wastes and also 
imposing zero discharge policies.

Health problems due to use of Endosulfan in Kerala 
554. SHRI K. CHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a large number of villagers are suffering 
from serious health problems due to the use of Endosulfan in the 
plantation areas of Kasargod district in Kerala; 
(b) if so, the details alongwith the nature of diseases and the number 
of people affected so far; 
124 

[16 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether any compensation has been provided to the victims, if 
so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the details of steps taken by Government to protect the people 
in this area? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) 
According to a study report of July 2002, submitted by National Institute 
of Occupational Health, Ahmedabad which carried out an epidemiological 
study in Padre village of Kasargod di strict of Kerala, a possible link was 
found between the higher prevalence of various ailments including Neuro 
behavioral disorders, congenital malformation in female subjects and 
abnormalities related to male re-pr oductive system in the Padre Village 
with the aerial spray of Endosulfan.  However, Dubey Committee set up 
by Ministry of Agriculture and Cooperation, in its report of July, 2003, 
has concluded that there is no link established between use of Endosulfan 
in Plantation Corporation of Kerala (PCK) plantations and health problems 
reported in Padre Village of Kasar god Distt. of Kerala. The committee 
inter alia recommended to conduct compre hensive, well designed and 
detailed health and epidemiological study in entire cashew plantation 
area of Kerala to ascertain the incidence of diseases in Padre vis-a-vis 
Kerala State average and also in the event of incidence of unusual health 
problem to determine probable factors responsible for alleged health 
problems. It also recommended that use of Endosulfan be continued as 
per provisions of Insecticides Act 1968 but aerial spraying of Endosulfan 
may not be allowed in any situation including in PCK plantations to ensure 
full safety. Further, as per Governme nt of Kerala, an expert committee 
constituted under the Chairmanship of Dr. P.K. Sivaraman, Addl. Director 
of Health Services of Government of Kerala in its report submitted in 
August, 2003, has stated that it could not find any other reason other 
than Endosulfan spraying to explain the reported health hazard. The 
State Government temporarily banned aerial spraying of Endosulfan and 
declared pesticide holiday for five years. The Hon'ble High Court of Kerala 
in its order dated 12.8.2002 in O.P. No. 16300/01 has stayed the use of 
Endosulfan in the State. The State Government is providing free treatment 
to those, suffering from the reported problems and providing free 
medicine to the poor patients.
